content:
A Class 11 Maths Term-1 test is the first paper that tells you the truth. Not whether you have read the chapters — whether you can actually use them under a clock. I have watched plenty of bright students in Jaipur and Pune breeze through homework all September, then lose fifteen marks in a Term-1 test to nothing more sinister than a rushed trigonometry value or a permutation they read too fast. The chapters were not the problem. The exam habits were.

This post is a focused walk-through of a CBSE-style Class 11 Term-1 test: the exact chapters it pulls from, how the marks are usually split, what to revise first, and how to squeeze real learning out of a practice paper. At the end there is a free 8-question quiz — fresh questions, one from each core area — so you can find your weak spot today rather than in the exam hall.

Which chapters a Class 11 Term-1 test covers

Term 1 sits on the opening block of the NCERT syllabus. Schools shuffle the order slightly, but a CBSE Class 11 Maths Term-1 test almost always draws from these six:

  • Sets — subsets and power sets, Venn diagrams, and the union formula n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B).
  • Relations and Functions — Cartesian products, what makes a relation a function, and finding domain and range.
  • Trigonometric Functions — radian measure, the standard angle values, signs across the four quadrants, and the core identities.
  • Complex Numbers — the powers of i, conjugate and modulus, and roots when the discriminant turns negative.
  • Linear Inequalities — solving one-variable inequalities and reading the solution off a number line.
  • Permutations and Combinations — the fundamental counting principle, factorials, and the line between order-matters and order-does-not.

Notice what is not here. Sequences and Series, Straight Lines and the Binomial Theorem usually belong to the later part of the year, so a true Term-1 paper leaves them out. Always cross-check against your own school circular — but if you drill these six cold, you have covered the reliable core.

What each chapter tends to ask

Term-1 questions are more predictable than students expect. Here is the shape of what typically comes from each area, so your revision has a target.

How the marks are usually split

A Term-1 test follows the same skeleton as the CBSE board blueprint, scaled to whatever total your school sets. Whether it is out of 40 or the full 80, the section pattern rarely changes: a block of 1-mark objective questions, some 2- and 3-mark short answers, a couple of 5-mark long answers, and a 4-mark case study.

The part students underrate every time is the 1-mark section. On an 80-mark paper that is a full quarter of the total decided by quick recall and small calculations — a careless slip there stings exactly as much as a wrong long-answer. Treat the objective questions as marks you cannot afford to leak, not as a warm-up.

How to prepare for a Class 11 Term-1 test

I will skip the ‘study harder’ advice and tell you what actually shifts a score.

Automate the standard values

Trigonometric ratios for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, the four-step cycle of powers of i (i, −1, −i, 1), and the subset rule 2n turn up in almost every Term-1 paper. If you can recall them without thinking, the objective section becomes free marks.

Do the NCERT exercises with a pen

Complex numbers and permutations especially punish passive reading. You can follow a worked P&C solution perfectly and still freeze when the numbers change. Solve, do not just review. The NCERT Class 11 Mathematics textbook is the free official source, and the exam design comes straight from CBSE.

Practise against a timer

Once the exercises feel routine, sit a full paper under time. A minute a mark is a fair rule, leaving a few minutes at the end to recheck the one-markers. If a long-answer is not moving after four minutes, flag it and go — chasing one hard proof while three easy questions sit unread is the classic way to lose marks you had already earned.

How to use a practice test properly

A mock is only worth the time if you treat it like the real thing and then mine it afterwards. My routine:

  • Time it. Give yourself a fixed window and do not pause the clock.
  • Attempt everything before you check anything. Marking answer-by-answer flatters your score and teaches you nothing.
  • Sort your errors. Every wrong answer is either a concept gap or a careless slip — revise for the first, slow down for the second.
  • Redo the misses from a blank page a day later. If you can, the fix has stuck.

One honest caveat: never judge yourself on a single test. Scores swing with the exact questions. It is the pattern across three or four attempts — which chapter keeps costing you marks — that tells you where to spend your final week.

quiz.title: Class 11 Maths Term-1 Test Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight fresh questions, one from each Term-1 chapter — sets, relations and functions, trigonometry, complex numbers, inequalities, permutations and combinations. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: CBSE Class 11 Maths Term-1 core chapters

questions.q: If n(A) = 15, n(B) = 10 and n(A∩B) = 5, what is n(A∪B)?
If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {a, b}, how many elements are in A×B?
questions.explanation: n(A×B) = n(A) × n(B) = 3 × 2 = 6. Every element of A pairs with every element of B.

questions.q: What is the value of i³?
questions.explanation: i³ = i² × i = (−1) × i = −i. The powers of i cycle every four: i, −1, −i, 1.
Subtract 3: 2x < 6. Divide by 2 (positive, so the sign stays): x < 3.

questions.q: In how many ways can the 5 letters of the word DELHI (all different) be arranged?
questions.explanation: All five letters are distinct, so the number of arrangements is 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

questions.q: What is the value of C(6, 4), the number of ways to choose 4 items from 6?
questions.explanation: C(6, 4) = 6! / (4! × 2!) = (6 × 5) / (2 × 1) = 15. Order does not matter, so it is a combination.

questions.q: A relation from set A to set B is defined as a subset of which set?
questions.explanation: A relation from A to B is a subset of the Cartesian product A×B — each ordered pair takes its first element from A and its second from B.

faq.q: Which chapters come in a Class 11 Maths Term-1 test?
faq.a: Most CBSE schools test the opening block: Sets, Relations and Functions, Trigonometric Functions, Complex Numbers, Linear Inequalities, and Permutations and Combinations. Sequences and Series, Straight Lines and the Binomial Theorem usually belong to Term 2, but always confirm from your school’s syllabus circular.

faq.q: How is a Class 11 Term-1 test marked?
faq.a: It follows the CBSE section pattern scaled to your school’s total — 1-mark objective questions, 2- and 3-mark short answers, 5-mark long answers, and a 4-mark case study. The 1-mark section is worth guarding: on an 80-mark paper it is a full quarter of the marks.

faq.q: What should I revise first for the Term-1 test?
faq.a: Lock down the recall-heavy facts — trigonometric standard values, the powers of i, and the 2 to the power n subset rule. These appear on almost every paper and turn the objective section into easy marks. Then work the NCERT exercises by hand before attempting a timed paper.

faq.q: How is this different from a mid-term mock test?
faq.a: A Term-1 test is narrower — it focuses on just the first block of chapters and skips Sequences and Series. Treat it as a checkpoint on the six core topics rather than a full half-year rehearsal, and use it to catch a weak chapter early.
